steps.body:
The **average rate of change** of f over [a, b] is the slope of the **secant line** joining (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)):

(f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a).

It's the familiar rise-over-run (recall slope), now measuring how fast f changes on average across an interval — like average speed over a trip.

widget.prompt: On y = x³, set the gap to 1 — the interval from x = 1 to x = 2 — and read the average rate.
widget.successFeedback: Rise 7 over run 1 = 7. It is a single number standing in for everything the curve did between 1 and 2, and the curve did a great deal.
widget.lowFeedback: The gap is under 1 — B has not reached x = 2.
widget.highFeedback: The gap is over 1 — B has gone past x = 2.

predict.prompt: You'll build the secant from A at x = 1 out to B at x = 2 on y = x³. Compared with the tangent slope AT A (3), the secant's slope will be…
predict.reveal: The secant's slope is (f(2) − f(1))/1 = 7, against 3 for the tangent at A. On a curve whose slope keeps growing, the stretch out to B crosses steeper ground than A itself — so the average beats the value at the start.

cml.actionGoal: Shrink the interval between two points and compare secant slope with the limiting tangent slope.

explanationVariants: Rise 21 over run 3 gives an average rate of 7.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = x², find the average rate of change on [2, 5].

commonErrors.feedback: 21 = 25 − 4 is the rise alone. Divide by the run 3: 21/3 = 7.
3 is the run. Average rate = rise/run = 21/3 = 7.

steps.body: Notice the average rate DEPENDS on the interval: x² averaged 4 on [1, 3] but 7 on [2, 5] — steeper further right. A secant only reports the overall change between two points; it can't tell you the rate at a single instant. That gap is what the next lesson closes.

explanationVariants: Writing b = a + h, the average rate becomes (f(a + h) − f(a))/h — the difference quotient, the same secant slope with step size h.
The difference quotient is just rise/run with run named h.

widget.prompt: The average rate of change (f(a + h) − f(a))/h is also called the:

options.label: difference quotient
options.feedback: Right — it's the secant slope written with step size h.

options.label: product rule
options.feedback: That's a later derivative rule. This secant-slope expression is the difference quotient.

options.label: limit law
options.feedback: Limit laws combine limits. This rise-over-run expression is the difference quotient.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = x², compute the difference quotient at a = 2 with h = 1: (f(2 + 1) − f(2))/1.

commonErrors.feedback: f(3) − f(2) = 9 − 4 = 5 (don't forget to subtract f(2)).

explanationVariants: At a = 2 with h = 0.5: (f(2.5) − f(2))/0.5 = (6.25 − 4)/0.5 = 2.25/0.5 = 4.5 — closer to the instantaneous value than h = 1 gave.
Smaller h (0.5) yields 4.5, nearing the true instantaneous rate at x = 2.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = x² at a = 2 with h = 0.5, compute (f(2.5) − f(2))/0.5.

commonErrors.feedback: 5 was the h = 1 answer. With h = 0.5: (6.25 − 4)/0.5 = 4.5.

takeaways: Average rate of change = secant slope (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
With b = a + h it's the difference quotient (f(a + h) − f(a))/h.
Shrinking h nudges the secant toward a single-point rate.
steps.teaser: Next: take h → 0 and get the instantaneous rate — the derivative.

concept.body: Average rate of change over [a,b] = (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a), the secant slope. With b=a+h it is the difference quotient (f(a+h)−f(a))/h.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = x², find the average rate of change on [1, 2].

commonErrors.feedback: 4 = f(2) alone. Subtract f(1) and divide: (4 − 1)/1 = 3.
